prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker expresses a desperate need for an immediate and invaluable experience found in the present moment.
- The sight of orange marigolds against a pink garage door and green surroundings overwhelms the mind with uncontrollable beauty.
- The poem suggests that scientific explanations of light and color cannot account for the felt experience of beauty.
- The speaker contrasts the value of beauty with material objects, food, art, and money, insisting that its worth cannot be measured.
- The final lines imply that the speaker has sacrificed everything for this intense, penetrating experience of beauty.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker confronts a desperate need to account for the overwhelming experience of beauty, using the immediate sight of orange marigolds against a pink garage door as a meditation on perception, language, value, and explanation. The poem finds that beauty’s effect on the mind is inescapable, priceless, and impossible to reduce to science or economics, making it both spiritually invaluable and materially ruinous.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Anything, Desperately, But

outputs.L1:
I need everything else—anything else—desperately.  
But I have nothing,  
shall have nothing but this:  
immediate, inescapable, and invaluable.  

No one can afford THIS,  
being made here and now  
(Seattle, Washington, 17 May 1955).  

MARIGOLDS.  

Concise, wooden, orange.  
Behind them, the garage door:  
pink  
(paint sold under a fatuous name, “Old Rose,”  
which brings a war to mind).  

And the mind slides over the fence again:  
orange against pink and green.  
Uncontrollable!  
Returned of its own accord,  
it can explain nothing,  
give no account.  

What good?  
What worth?  

Dying!  
You have less than a second  
to live,  
to try to explain:  

Say that light, in particular wavelengths  
or bundles wobbling at a given speed,  
produces the experience:  
orange against pink.  

Better than a sirloin steak?  
A screen by Korin?  

The effect of this, taken internally—  
the effect of beauty on the mind—  
has no equivalent, least of all  
in these objects,  
which ought to manifest  
a surface disorientation, pitting,  
or striae,  
admitting some plausible interpretation.  

But the cost  
can’t be expressed in numbers  
dodging between a vagrancy rap  
and the newest electrical brain-curette;  
eating what the rich are bullied into giving,  
or what the poor willingly share,  
depriving themselves.  

More expensive than ambergris,  
although the stink isn’t as loud.  
(A few wise men have said,  
“Produced the same way . . .  
vomited out by sick whales.”)  

Valuable for the same qualities:  
staying power and penetration.  

I’ve squandered every crying dime.
outputs.L2:
I want all the remaining things—  
whatever is left—  
with urgency, almost painfully.  

Yet I possess nothing,  
and will possess nothing except this:  
something immediate, unavoidable, beyond price.  
No one is able to pay for THIS,  
which is coming into existence right here, right now  
in Seattle, Washington, on May 17, 1955.  

MARIGOLDS.  

Brief, solid, almost wooden.  
Orange.  

Behind them stands the garage door,  
pink—  
paint marketed under the foolish label “Old Rose,”  
a name that calls up thoughts of war.  

Then the mind slips once more across the fence:  
orange set against pink and green.  
Impossible to govern!  
It returns by itself.  

It cannot clarify anything.  
It offers no explanation.  
What use is it?  
What value?  

Perishing!  
There is less than one second left  
to remain alive,  
to attempt an explanation:  

Say, perhaps, that light—  
specific wavelengths, or packets  
shaking along at a certain velocity—  
creates the sensation of  
orange against pink.  

Is it better than a sirloin steak?  
Better than a screen by Korin?  

What happens when this is taken inward—  
what beauty does to the mind—  
has no substitute,  
least of all these physical things,  
which should reveal  
some disturbance of surface,  
some pocking,  
some streaking,  
something that might allow  
a reasonable interpretation.  

But its cost  
cannot be put into figures,  
not while one is dodging between  
a charge of vagrancy  
and the latest electric curette for the brain,  
eating whatever the wealthy are pressured into handing over,  
or what the poor give freely,  
going without in order to share.  

It is dearer than ambergris,  
though its smell is not as forceful.  

A handful of wise men have remarked:  
“Made in the same manner . . .  
thrown up by sick whales.”  

It is precious for identical reasons:  
its persistence,  
and its power to enter deeply.  

I have wasted every last miserable cent.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who feels an urgent, almost desperate need for a powerful experience available only in the present moment. This experience is not something abstract or distant; it is immediate, physical, and overwhelming. The speaker seems to believe that what is being encountered now is invaluable, something that cannot be postponed, possessed, or replaced.

At the center of this experience is the sight of orange marigolds set against a pink garage door, surrounded by green. The vivid contrast of these colors overwhelms the speaker’s mind. The beauty of the scene is not calm or decorative; it is intense, almost uncontrollable. The speaker is struck by the way ordinary objects and colors suddenly become extraordinary, filling the mind with a force that cannot be contained or fully understood.

The poem also suggests that scientific explanations are inadequate when faced with the felt experience of beauty. Light and color may be described in terms of waves, reflection, or perception, but such explanations do not capture what it is like to be pierced by beauty in the moment. The speaker implies that science can explain how the eye sees color, but not why a particular arrangement of colors can feel so necessary, astonishing, and emotionally powerful.

Throughout the poem, the speaker contrasts the value of beauty with the value of material things. Beauty is compared to objects, food, art, and money, yet it exceeds them all. It cannot be bought, eaten, collected, or measured in ordinary terms. Its worth is beyond practical usefulness or financial calculation. The speaker insists that the experience of beauty has a value that surpasses possessions and even traditional forms of artistic value.

By the final lines, the poem implies that the speaker has given up everything for this intense encounter. The experience of beauty is portrayed as penetrating and absolute, something that enters the speaker deeply and demands total surrender. In this sense, the poem becomes not just a description of marigolds, color, or light, but a meditation on the overwhelming power of beauty and the human need to be transformed by it.
outputs.L4:
The speaker is driven by an urgent need to explain what happens when beauty overwhelms the mind. The occasion is ordinary and immediate: the sight of orange marigolds set against a pink garage door. Yet this simple visual encounter becomes the starting point for a much larger meditation on perception, language, value, and the limits of explanation. The flowers and the door are not treated merely as objects in a scene; they become evidence of how intensely the world can strike the senses and how difficult it is to translate that intensity into words.

The poem suggests that beauty is not passive or decorative. It acts upon the observer. Once perceived, it cannot simply be dismissed, ignored, or neatly categorized. The speaker feels compelled to account for it, but every available system of explanation seems inadequate. Scientific description may identify color, light, surface, and the mechanics of vision, but it cannot fully explain why the sight matters so much. Economic language may try to assign value, but beauty resists being priced. It is “priceless” not because it has no effect on value, but because its value exceeds the terms by which value is usually measured.

At the same time, the poem recognizes that beauty is not harmless. Its power may be spiritually sustaining, even necessary, but it is also destabilizing. To be seized by beauty is to be taken out of ordinary usefulness and practicality. The experience enriches the mind while also making ordinary material calculations seem insufficient or even absurd. In this sense, beauty becomes both a kind of wealth and a kind of ruin: it gives the speaker something invaluable, but it also disrupts the systems—scientific, linguistic, economic—through which people usually try to make sense of the world.

Ultimately, the poem presents beauty as an inescapable force. The marigolds against the garage door cannot be reduced to an explanation, yet they demand one. The speaker’s struggle to describe them reveals the central paradox of the experience: beauty feels absolutely real and necessary, but it cannot be fully possessed, measured, or translated. Its meaning lies precisely in its resistance to being contained.
outputs.L5:
**Anything, Desperately, But**

She said she would do anything.

Anything to leave the silence behind, anything to stop the slow ache of waiting, anything to feel like the world was still wide and open. She had spent too many nights staring at the ceiling, desperately searching for a reason to stay exactly where she was.

But life rarely changes all at once.

It begins in small moments: a packed bag by the door, a message left unanswered, a decision made before fear can argue. She did not know where she was going, and she did not have a perfect plan. But she knew she could no longer remain in a place that made her feel invisible.

So she stepped outside.

The morning air was cold, sharp enough to wake her fully. For the first time in a long time, she felt uncertain — but alive. And maybe that was enough. Maybe she did not need to have everything figured out. Maybe she only needed the courage to begin.

She would do anything to find herself again.

Desperately, quietly, bravely.

But this time, she would do it for herself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental free-verse poem in a mid-century American style, set in Seattle on May 17, 1955, centered on marigolds, color perception, beauty, poverty, and desperation.
counterfactuals.output:
**May 17, 1955 — Seattle**

Rain loosens its gray mouth  
over Yesler, over the docks,  
over the woman counting nickels  
in the bakery window’s reflection.

May 17.  
The calendar says spring  
but the city wears an old coat.

In a coffee can by the boardinghouse steps  
marigolds burn—  
small municipal suns,  
orange as streetcar sparks,  
yellow as the last pat of butter  
in a poor man’s dish.

Who taught the eye  
to call this color beautiful?

The eye, that clerk of hunger,  
that tired photographer  
developing the world in chemicals  
of want.

A child says gold.  
His mother says don’t touch.  
A painter passing under an umbrella  
says cadmium, chrome, vermilion.  
The old man on the stoop says nothing—  
he has seen eggs go scarce,  
coal go dear,  
hands go useless in the damp.

Still the marigolds insist.

Their heads crowd together  
like dockworkers at hiring time,  
bright caps in the rain,  
each one asking for the day’s wage  
of sunlight.

Seattle smells of wet wool,  
fish scales, coffee grounds,  
gasoline on puddles—  
rainbows there too,  
thin and poisonous,  
beauty leaking from machines.

What is color  
to the woman pawning her wedding ring  
on Second Avenue?

What is beauty  
to the man sleeping upright  
in the mission chapel,  
mouth open as if singing  
or drowning?

Yet look—  
the marigolds do not apologize  
for being extravagant.

They have no rent.  
No teeth to fix.  
No letter from the county.  
No landlord knocking  
with his soft white fist.

They squander orange  
on the broken step,  
throw yellow into the weather,  
make a little riot  
against the bookkeeping of despair.

And the rain,  
which has washed so many faces  
anonymous,  
cannot wash them pale.

I stand there,  
not rich enough for kindness,  
not poor enough for sainthood,  
my eyes full of borrowed fire.

The city leans down  
with its damp warehouses,  
its neon not yet lit,  
its gulls like torn paper  
over Elliott Bay.

Someone is hungry.  
Someone is beautiful.  
Someone is selling their last good shoes.  
Someone is naming a flower  
as if naming could save it.

Marigold—  
Mary’s gold—  
cheap blossom, altar scrap,  
coin of the vacant lot.

On May 17, 1955,  
in Seattle,  
under the colorless labor of rain,  
they open and open,

desperate little engines  
of seeing,

saying:

even here  
even now  
look harder.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense modernist prose-poem about seeing orange marigolds against a pink garage door, mixing scientific language about light with reflections on value, hunger, and art.
counterfactuals.output:
Orange marigolds before the pink garage door: an event of photons, not a scene, a small riot of wavelengths thrown against painted wood, reflected, absorbed, misread by the hungering cones of the eye. The petals burn not because they are fire but because they refuse portions of the spectrum, keeping nothing of orange except its abandonment into me. Pink, that domesticated blush of rust and milk, holds the flat plane behind them like a cheap iconostasis, and the flowers—coin-faced, ragged, municipal, almost vulgar—become suddenly priceless. Value begins here: in contrast, in scarcity, in the body’s old arithmetic of wanting what glows.

I stand before the garage, which is also a wall, which is also capital, storage, enclosure, a mouth shut on tools and oil and bicycles, while the marigolds spend themselves openly, photosynthetic and prodigal, eating light with their green machinery, making sugar out of radiance, making beauty as a by-product of survival. Hunger is not opposed to art. Hunger is the root under the color, the dark equation in the soil: nitrogen, water, carbon, need. The eye too is hungry, licking the edges of things, converting distance into possession and failing, always failing, which is why looking hurts and why it is necessary.

What is a marigold worth against a garage door? Less than the house, less than the land, less than the car sleeping inside; more than all of them for one instant, because it solves the afternoon. The pigments declare their chemistry—carotenoids, anthocyanins, the tender fraud of surfaces—yet the declaration becomes lyric, becomes a small orange theorem: that matter under light can exceed its price. Art is this excess, this refusal to remain inventory. A flower, a door, the retina’s wet cinema; and somewhere within the skull, poverty and appetite kneel together before the incandescent ordinary, asking to be fed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that feels like a discovered notebook entry: urgent, fragmented, philosophical, with the phrase “Seattle, Washington 17 May, 1955” and imagery of marigolds, old rose paint, whales, ambergris, and squandered money.
counterfactuals.output:
Seattle, Washington 17 May, 1955

found this under the bed—
not the bed but the idea of one,
a plank of sleep, old rose paint flaking
from the rented wall like a second skin
I have failed to deserve.

Marigolds in a jar.
Who brought them?
Who spends yellow so recklessly
on the dying?

Rain worrying the window.
Harbor below, black with departures.
The whales are out there
with their cathedral lungs,
dragging whole planets through the cold,
and we—small accountants of breath—
argue over squandered money,
coins gone to cigarettes, coffee,
a ticket never used,
a room with no future in it.

What is a life
but the receipt we keep smoothing flat?

Ambergris: the sea’s strange treasure,
sickness made precious,
wound turned perfume.
Remember this.
Remember that even the whale’s grief
can wash ashore
and be weighed in a merchant’s hand.

I wanted to be pure.
Instead I was expensive.
Instead I bought flowers
and let them burn down
in a chipped blue jar.

If anyone finds this—
no, listen:
the soul is not saved by thrift.
Nor by hunger.
Nor by the beautiful lie
that suffering pays us back.

Outside, gulls tear the morning open.

Inside, the old rose wall.
The marigolds.
My pockets empty
as a sermon after the fire.

I am writing quickly
because the world is leaving,
because the world is always leaving,
because somewhere in the dark water
a whale rises
with its mouth full of night
and does not ask
what anything was worth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an ekphrastic, Beat-era-style poem about the overwhelming mental effect of beauty, comparing flowers and color to steak, Japanese screens, electrical brain treatments, and the lives of the poor.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gallery Shock**

I stood before the flowers in the museum—  
not flowers exactly but an explosion wearing petals,  
a butcher’s window of red, marbled light,  
roses like steak laid raw on the mind,  
fat-veined, holy, unreasonable,  
the kind of color that makes the brain  
put down its little fork and tremble.

Behind them, flat gold trembled too—  
a Japanese screen of weather and cranes,  
silk air, lacquer dusk,  
each blossom pinned to eternity  
like a rich man’s quiet idea of spring.  
And I, poor in my shoes,  
felt beauty enter without knocking.

It came on like voltage—  
not inspiration, no,  
more like the old white room,  
the straps, the bite-block,  
the bright official lightning  
they once sent through sorrow  
to teach it a new name.

Color did that.  
Yellow snapped its switch.  
Blue burned down the hallway of the skull.  
Green opened a tenement window  
where a woman rinsed one cup for three children,  
and even the dishwater shone  
like it had been forgiven.

O unbearable bouquet!  
You hang there in silence  
while men sleep under bridges,  
while paychecks vanish into rent,  
while mothers count coins by the stove—  
and still your crimson keeps singing,  
still your impossible orange  
throws a banquet in the nerves.

Beauty is not gentle.  
It is meat, silk, current, hunger.  
It is the poor man’s feast and punishment,  
the screen he cannot own,  
the shock he cannot refuse,  
the flower opening inside his head  
until the whole dark room  
is blooming, blooming, blooming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a chaotic first-person poem in which the speaker tries and fails to explain why orange marigolds against pink and green are invaluable, using abrupt line breaks, parentheticals, and references to science, wealth, poverty, and ambergris.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep trying to say it—

orange marigolds  
against pink  
against green

are worth more than—  
(no, not gold, gold is too obedient)

more than the little equations
we pin to the frog of the world  
and call it science.

Listen:

chlorophyll takes the sun  
and chews it into sugar  
and somewhere in that green mouth  
the orange happens,  
a flare, a cough,  
a small municipal fire—

and the pink behind it  
(what is pink doing there?)  
makes the orange unbearable.

I mean invaluable.

I mean I have no money.

I mean once I counted coins  
in a laundromat  
while someone’s child screamed  
like a rusted hinge  
and outside, in a cracked tire,  
marigolds burned and burned  
as if poverty were only  
a bad translation of light.

No, that’s not right.

A banker would not understand  
unless the banker had once knelt  
in dirt  
and smelled the hot peppery heads  
of those flowers  
and thought: ambergris.

Yes, ambergris—  
whale-stomach treasure,  
ocean vomit,  
perfume’s secret dirty saint—

the way value arrives
from illness, accident,
depth,
rot,
time.

(Do you see?)

The marigolds are orange  
because physics.  
Because photons.  
Because electrons leap  
like thieves over fences.  
Because my grandmother’s hands  
were brown and split  
and planted them anyway.  
Because green is the body  
and pink is the embarrassing heart  
and orange is the shout  
that ruins the funeral.

I am explaining badly.

If I owned a palace  
I would trade it for one wet morning  
with those flowers  
shaking in their beds.

If I owned nothing  
(which is closer)  
I would still be robbed  
by seeing them.

They are not priceless  
like diamonds are “priceless”  
in a locked room  
with a guard  
and a camera  
and a velvet little lie.

They are priceless like bread  
when you are hungry.

Priceless like breath  
after panic.

Priceless like the whale  
not knowing  
what the perfumer knows.

Orange marigolds  
against pink  
against green—

I can’t finish.

The colors keep interrupting me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
